claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring controllable multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed method combines DFT-derived intrinsic parameters with experimentally determined statistical microstructure descriptors in a multi-fidelity machine-learning surrogate.
The surrogate can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Elastic constants, misfit volumes, surface energies, and unstable stacking-fault energies are relevant first-principles inputs for models of alloy strengthening and ductility.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations mediate the relationship between atomic-scale DFT inputs and macroscopic mechanical response.
Statistical microstructure descriptors allow the model to capture mesoscale effects that intrinsic DFT parameters alone do not capture.
Fusing intrinsic DFT outputs with microstructure descriptors bridges atomic and mesoscale behavior and improves mechanical-property prediction reliability.
The proposed surrogate will be more accurate than conventional high-throughput DFT or CALPHAD methods for the three target mechanical properties.
The proposed surrogate will be more computationally efficient than conventional high-throughput DFT or CALPHAD approaches.
Predictive accuracy will improve by approximately 20–30% over traditional methods.
Computational time will be reduced by approximately one order of magnitude.
Predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness will be within ±15% of experimental measurements when training data comprehensively cover heterostructural variability.
The method is reliable under room-temperature tensile and fracture testing when the hierarchical microstructure is preserved and its statistics are representative.
The method may also be reliable at elevated temperatures if it is appropriately calibrated.
Model reliability depends on having a sufficiently large and compositionally diverse training set.
Unrepresentative microstructure statistics, unanticipated phase transformations, or extreme local compositional deviations will reduce model reliability.
The method will lose reliability if its DFT parameters omit essential bonding or defect mechanisms specific to the hierarchical state.
Ab initio calculations are time-consuming, and CALPHAD can require significant computational resources.
Explicit prediction of alloy fracture or yield strength is generally beyond available DFT implementations.
Prior high-throughput and metric-based alloy-screening methods have not adequately explored complex relationships between multiple metrics and thermomechanical properties.
